turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she had no desire to discuss Mr. Wickham’s affairs further, as she was already well acquainted with his side of the story and found it entirely credible.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that he would not further discuss Mr Wickham’s affairs, as the truth was far from what Elizabeth believed.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that if his explanation of Mr Wickham’s character was true, she could only pity the gentleman for having so unworthy a representative.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that his explanation of Mr Wickham’s character was truthful and wished to move on from the unpleasant subject.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she could not pretend to understand his feelings, as his actions had given her reason to dislike him, and his explanation did little to change that impression.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that his actions, though not as open and affectionate as Elizabeth might have wished, were governed by his sense of propriety and duty, and that his feelings for her were sincere and profound.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that despite his explanation, her dislike for him was too strong to be easily overcome and his affection for her seemed unlikely to alter her feelings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that his feelings for Elizabeth were not easily swayed by her disapproval and that he would continue to regard her with the utmost esteem and affection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that his declaration of affection, though unexpected, did not change her opinion of him and that his continued regard would be in vain unless accompanied by a change in his behaviour and manners.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that his true sentiments towards Elizabeth were not to be easily dismissed and that he would strive to amend his behaviour and manners in light of her criticisms.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she appreciated his willingness to consider her criticisms but doubted the sincerity of his intentions if they did not stem from a genuine desire to improve himself.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he would prove his sincerity through his actions and that he hoped she would one day see his true character and intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that while she appreciated his words, his actions would need to speak louder than his declarations if he hoped to earn her regard and respect.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted to Elizabeth that he would work tirelessly to earn her respect and would not rest until she saw the true man he aimed to be.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that her feelings towards him were rooted in his past actions and that mere words would not suffice to change them.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he understood her distrust and would do everything in his power to change her perception of him, acknowledging the depth of her feelings towards him.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she would observe his actions closely and that only time would tell if his words were sincere and his intentions genuine.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he would prove himself through his actions and that she would see the change in him, hoping to earn her esteem and affection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she appreciated his earnestness but warned him that she would not be swayed easily and that he must earn her trust through consistent and genuine efforts.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he would work diligently to earn her trust and respect, vowing to be a better man in her eyes.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that he had struggled in vain and that it would not do. His feelings would not be repressed, and he must allow him to tell her how ardently he admired and loved her.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that in such cases, it was believed to be the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It was natural that obligation should be felt, and if she could feel gratitude, she would now thank him. But she could not, for she had never desired his good opinion, and he had certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. She was sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone, but it had been most unconsciously done and she hoped it would be of short duration. The feelings which he told her had long prevented the acknowledgment of his regard could have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that this was all the reply which he was to have the honour of expecting. He might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, he was thus rejected. But it was of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she might as well ask why, with such a clear intention of offending and insulting her, he chose to tell her that he liked her against his will, against his reason, and even against his character. Was not this some excuse for incivility, if she was uncivil? But she had other provocations. He knew she had. Had not her own feelings decided against him, had they been indifferent, or even favourable, did he think that any consideration would tempt her to accept the man who had been the means of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she had every reason in the world to think ill of him. No motive could excuse the unjust and ungenerous part he had acted there. He dared not, he could not deny that he had been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that it was not merely this affair on which her dislike was founded. Long before it had taken place, her opinion of him was decided. His character was unfolded in the recital which she had received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what could he have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship could he here defend himself? Or under what misrepresentation could he here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that she took an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that who that knew what his misfortunes had been could help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that his misfortunes had indeed been great indeed.
